title: Chart of Accounts 101: What Accounts Every SaaS Startup Actually Needs In 2026
summary: Build a SaaS chart of accounts with sample account numbers, revenue and expense categories, and rules for prepaid credits, deferred revenue, and payment fees.
body_markdown:
A chart of accounts is the list of accounts you use to record transactions. For a SaaS business, it should show what customers owe, what you have earned, what you still owe customers, and what it costs to provide the service.


Start with a small set of accounts. Add detail when it helps you close the books, file a return, or make a decision. Use customer, product, and department fields for detail that does not need its own general ledger account.


## SaaS chart of accounts template


The numbers below are examples. They are not required account codes. Copy the rows that fit your business and have your accountant confirm how you should classify each balance.


Example code Account Type What belongs here


1000 Operating cash Asset Money in your bank account


1010 Payment processor clearing Asset Customer payments awaiting payout, less amounts settled


1100[Accounts receivable](https://www.afternoon.co/blog/accounts-receivable-SaaS) Asset Amounts customers owe under an unconditional right to payment


1110 Allowance for credit losses Contra asset Estimated losses on receivables under your accounting policy


1200 Prepaid software and API services Asset Unused vendor services paid for in advance


1300 Equipment Asset Qualifying equipment costs


1310 Accumulated depreciation Contra asset Depreciation recorded against equipment


2000 Accounts payable Liability Supplier bills you owe


2100 Accrued expenses Liability Costs incurred before the supplier bill arrives


2200 Deferred revenue Liability Customer payments or billings for service you still owe


2300 Sales tax payable Liability Tax collected that you owe to tax authorities


2400 Payroll liabilities Liability Withholdings and other unpaid payroll amounts


3000 Contributed capital Equity Owners' investment, using accounts suited to your entity


3100 Retained earnings Equity Prior earnings retained in the business


4000 Subscription revenue Revenue Subscription service earned during the period


4100 Usage revenue Revenue Metered service earned during the period


4200 Services revenue Revenue Earned implementation or other service fees


4900 Refunds and allowances Contra revenue Reductions to revenue, under your policy


5000 Production hosting Cost of revenue Infrastructure used to deliver the product


5100 Production API and model costs Cost of revenue Third-party usage tied to serving customers


6000 Research and development Operating expense Product work expensed under your policy


6100 Sales and marketing Operating expense Customer acquisition costs expensed under your policy


6200 General and administrative Operating expense Finance, legal, and other business overhead


These accounts give you a starting point, not a rule that every software cost belongs in one place. A model call used to serve a paying customer has a different purpose from a model call used to test a new feature.


## Accounts to add when the business needs them


The starter chart omits accounts that depend on your contracts, financing, and tax position. Add them when they represent a real balance or recurring reporting need.


Situation Accounts or detail to consider


Earned amounts with a conditional payment right Contract assets, kept separate from unconditional receivables


Refunds owed to customers Refund liability, with a schedule of open obligations


Credit cards or borrowing Credit card payable, notes payable, and accrued interest


Tax balances beyond sales tax Separate income and franchise tax payables where applicable


Payroll Wages, employer taxes, and benefits, with related unpaid balances


Office or equipment leases Security deposits, leasehold improvements, and applicable right-of-use assets and lease liabilities


Qualifying development or sales commission costs Separate asset and amortization accounts under the relevant capitalization policy


Equity funding Share capital and additional paid-in capital, or the accounts appropriate to your entity


Lease accounts need to follow the lease assessment. Rent expense alone may not capture the assets and liabilities required by[FASB Topic 842](https://fasb.org/projects/current-projects/leases-398331) .


Within operating expenses, retain enough detail to review payroll, contractors, internal software, legal fees, recruiting, travel, meals, rent, insurance, and depreciation. Departments can identify R&D, sales, and administration without creating a second account for every cost in every team.


Separate production infrastructure from internal tools. Apply a written policy to support costs and payment fees so the same cost does not move between cost of revenue and operating expenses from month to month.


## How to classify common SaaS transactions


### Annual subscriptions


Billing a customer for a year does not by itself mean you earned a year of revenue. Record the receivable or cash and the amount owed in future service. Recognize revenue as you meet the contract's obligations.


For an illustrative $1,200 annual subscription with a single service delivered evenly over twelve months, the monthly revenue would be $100. Real contracts can include distinct services, discounts, or variable fees that change that schedule. See our[usage-based revenue recognition guide](https://www.afternoon.co/blog/usage-based-pricing-guide) .


### Prepaid AI credits


Keep credits you buy separate from credits you sell.


Unused vendor credits may belong in prepaid expenses, subject to the rights and recoverability of the balance. Customer credits may create a contract liability until you provide the service or meet the conditions to recognize another amount.


Do not put every credit in “discounts.” A payment for future service is different from a price reduction. Our[token and credit accounting guide](https://www.afternoon.co/blog/token-based-pricing-guide) covers both sides.


### Payment processor fees


A net payout can include customer receipts, fees, refunds, disputes, and adjustments. Record those parts separately so the payout does not become your revenue figure.


For example, a $100 customer payment less a $3 fee produces $97 in cash. If the $100 was already recorded as a receivable, the payment clears that receivable; it does not create another $100 of revenue. Use a clearing account to reconcile the settlement.


Choose a fee classification that fits your reporting policy and apply it consistently. Do not change the classification just to improve[gross margin](https://www.afternoon.co/glossary/gross-margin) .


### Software and equipment purchases


A long useful life alone does not settle whether a cost qualifies for capitalization. The rules for equipment, purchased software, and software you build differ. Set a written capitalization policy with your accountant, including how you treat small purchases and internal development.


## Use tracking fields before adding accounts


Create separate accounts when the accounting treatment differs. Use tracking fields when the treatment stays the same but you need another view.


For example, keep one production API expense account and tag costs by provider and product. You can then report provider spend without adding an account for every model version.


Useful fields include department, product, customer, project, and location. Keep them stable enough to compare periods.


### Keep research and contractor records useful


Tag research wages and contractor work by project and retain payroll, invoices, and work records. An “R&D” account label does not establish that a cost qualifies for a tax credit.


If you review the[research credit against payroll tax](https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/research-credit-against-payroll-tax-for-small-businesses) , keep the supporting cost detail available for the preparer. Apply the eligibility and election rules separately from the ledger classification. Keep vendor identity and tax documentation with contractor records; a domestic or foreign expense account is not a substitute for that review.


Use clear account names and leave room between account codes for later additions. Review “Other” and “Miscellaneous” balances during close so recurring costs do not stay hidden there.


## Set up the chart


1. Map each current account to the proposed account.
2. Check that opening balances still agree with the prior balance sheet.
3. Assign an owner to each balance sheet reconciliation.
4. Document the policy for credits, refunds, hosting, and development costs.
5. Test a full month of invoices, payments, vendor bills, and settlements.
6. Review the[income statement](https://www.afternoon.co/glossary/profit-and-loss-statement) and[balance sheet](https://www.afternoon.co/glossary/balance-sheet) before closing old accounts.


Keep the records that support each entry. The[IRS recordkeeping guide](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/recordkeeping) explains the role of invoices, receipts, and other source records. Your book reporting and tax treatment may differ.


## What to reconcile at month-end


Balance Supporting record


Cash and processor clearing Bank statements, settlement reports, fees, and unresolved transfers


Receivables and allowance Customer aging, cash applications, disputes, and credit-loss review


Prepaid expenses Purchases, service consumed, remaining rights, and expiry review


Deferred revenue and customer credits Opening balances, billings or receipts, earned revenue, refunds, and other adjustments


Payables and accruals Open supplier bills, unbilled costs, and payroll reports


Sales tax payable Tax collected, adjustments, filed returns, and remittances


Equipment and other capitalized costs Additions, disposals, and depreciation or amortization schedules


Assign a preparer and reviewer for each material balance. Explain timing differences and carry open items forward with an owner rather than posting an unexplained adjustment to make two reports match.


## Common questions


### How many accounts does a SaaS company need?


Enough to separate different accounting treatments and answer recurring reporting questions. A longer chart is not inherently better. If an account stays empty or repeats another account, review whether you need it.


### Is deferred revenue an asset?


No. It generally records a duty to provide service after a customer has paid or been billed. Accounts receivable records a right to payment. The same contract can create both balances.


### Should every revenue plan have its own account?


Usually, a product or plan field gives better detail with less upkeep. Separate revenue accounts when you need to distinguish the nature of the revenue, such as subscriptions, usage, and services.
